title: For the ways of peace (Gittin 61a)
hookLine: the Talmud rules that poor non-Jews are fed and their sick visited, for the ways of peace
last: BERURIAH READ CLOSELY, AND THE PAGE KEPT HER.

cards: Feed the poor. Visit the sick. Bury the dead.

Familiar duties, done by neighbors, by burial societies, by the person who brings soup. The Talmud takes that list and adds a few words that change its size. Not only for the Jewish poor, the Jewish sick, the Jewish dead.
For non-Jews too, side by side with them. And it gives a reason in one short Hebrew phrase. Today's word is that reason.

teach.h: FEED, VISIT, BURY: ALONG WITH ISRAEL.
teach.b: For the ways of peace. In Hebrew, mipnei darkhei shalom. First, the ruling.

In tractate Gittin, the Talmud brings a teaching: the poor of non-Jews are supported along with the poor of Israel, their sick are visited along with the sick of Israel, and their dead are buried along with the dead of Israel, for the ways of peace.
Along with. Not after. Not instead.
Second, a phrase with a family. The Mishnah in the same tractate lists other rulings made for the ways of peace.
The Torah reading in synagogue goes first to a priest, then a Levite, then any other Jew, so nobody quarrels over who goes first. And poor non-Jews are not stopped from gleaning in the fields.

teach.h: SMALL RULES FOR A SHARED STREET.
teach.b: Small rules that keep a shared street calm. Third, the size of it. The Talmud goes further, and says the whole Torah is for the sake of the ways of peace.
Its proof is a verse from Proverbs about wisdom and Torah: "Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace." Fourth, two ways to hear it.

teach.h: PRACTICAL WISDOM, OR GOD'S OWN WAY?
teach.b: Some readers hear the phrase as practical wisdom: neighbors who are cared for stay neighbors.

Others, Maimonides among them, tie these rulings to a verse in the Psalms saying that God is good to all and has mercy on all his works, and to the Proverbs verse, as if to say the law is simply acting like its Giver.
Both readings live in the tradition. Either way, the soup goes to every door on the street.

how: Jewish food pantries, visiting committees and charities often serve neighbors of every background, and some cite the ruling 'for the ways of peace' as one reason.

games.q: what does “for the ways of peace” mean?
o: a prayer for peace said at the end of services
caring for non-Jews along with Jews, to keep peace
a polite way of saying let's stop arguing

games.q: for the ways of peace — tap the pairs.
p: feed, visit, bury, along with Israel
priest, then Levite, then any Jew

s: the Talmud rules that poor non-Jews are supported along with poor Jews
and their sick visited and their dead buried, for the ways of peace.
'for the ways of peace' is the reason for just one ruling
the Mishnah in Gittin lists several, like the order of the Torah reading.
the Talmud says only some laws are for the ways of peace
it says the whole Torah is, citing Proverbs: all her paths are peace.

games.q: you run a community's charity fund. poor non-Jewish neighbors come to the door along with the Jewish poor. what does the Talmud say?
o: support them along with the poor of Israel.
help them only once every Jewish need is met.
games.why: the teaching in Gittin says the poor of non-Jews are supported along with the poor of Israel, for the ways of peace.

practice: Picture your circle, family, friends, the people who share your faith or your table, and let your attention drift to its edge: a neighbor you only nod to, the person who delivers your packages, someone of another faith, or none.
Let one face come forward, and hold it with goodwill for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: For the ways of peace. Mipnei darkhei shalom: the Talmud's reason for feeding, visiting and burying non-Jews along with Jews. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: because of the ways of peace.

carryVoice: Your line: for the ways of peace. Along with, not after. Rest well.
